notes.overview: General LMU setup cause-and-effect the coach can cite for ANY car, distilled from community setup guides. Provenance tags: [broadly-agreed] corroborated across sources or matches sim convention; [single-source] one creator's opinion/number, treat as a starting point not a target; [LMU] specific to this game. Numeric values are stated starting points, not validated against current BoP/patches.
method: Order of changes: fuel + tire pressures first, then brakes (bias, migration, max pedal force), then springs/ride-height/rake for the aero platform, then dampers, then toe + ARBs for rotation, and diff + wing last. [broadly-agreed]

Change ONE parameter at a time, then run several consistent laps before reading the result. Stop raising a value at the first click where instability (not just discomfort) appears, then back off one click. [broadly-agreed]
Tune for a race stint, not a single qualifying lap: a good race setup is what you can repeat for many laps as tires fade, not what's fastest on fresh tires. Test long runs. [broadly-agreed]

Don't copy a setup blindly across track variants; kerb and layout changes alter what the car needs. Sprint favors lower ride height and sharper rotation on edge; endurance favors a calmer, more repeatable, slightly rear-stable balance. [single-source]

levers.Tire pressures: LMU generally rewards running pressures near their lowest viable point for predictable grip. Use brake ducting (more open = cooler) to hold the tire temperature window rather than chasing it with pressure. Hypercars are more temperature-sensitive; LMGT3 more tolerant. [single-source]
levers.Anti-roll bars (ARB): Stiffer front ARB -> more understeer but more stable/quicker-reacting entry. Softer front ARB -> more turn-in rotation but less entry stability and slower direction changes. Stiffer rear ARB -> more exit rotation but the rear can swing out and go unstable in fast corners. Softer rear ARB -> more planted, stable exit but less rotation. A common approach: keep rear ARB soft as a stability baseline and do most rotation tuning on the front ARB. [broadly-agreed shape]
levers.Springs: Softer front springs -> less understeer. Stiffer rear springs -> more on-throttle rotation. Too stiff overall -> nervous/skittish; too soft -> wallowing. GT3s tolerate softer, compliant springs (absorb kerbs, carry mechanical grip); Hypercars need a stiffer, stable aero platform or the floor stalls. Spring rate, ride height, and wing are one coupled system. [broadly-agreed shape]
levers.Ride height / rake: More rake (rear higher than front) -> more front grip at turn-in. Less rake (rear lower) -> pointier front, more oversteer risk. Hypercar ride height is a tight window: too low bottoms out and unsettles the car, too high loses downforce. [LMU] in-game ride heights are set STATIC without fuel, so the car rides lower on a full tank than the number suggests. Use packers to kill local bottoming on one kerb/compression instead of raising ride height everywhere. [single-source]
levers.Dampers (bump / rebound): Bump controls how the suspension takes kerbs/compression and weight transfer; rebound controls how it returns. Too stiff -> nervous; too soft -> wallowing. Iterative, circuit-by-circuit tuning by kerb behavior; no universal numbers. [broadly-agreed shape]
levers.Differential (preload / lock): More preload / on-power lock -> more stable off-corner traction but harder to rotate. Less lock -> better rotation but livelier, especially on worn tires. Excess turn-in rotation -> reduce preload; entry understeer -> increase lock. GT3 diffs feel friendlier; Hypercars (esp. with hybrid) get lively if run too open. [broadly-agreed shape]
levers.Aero / wing: More front aero -> crisper turn-in, less rear stability. More rear wing -> safer/more stable but harder to rotate mid-corner, and adds drag. LMGT3 is far less aero-dependent and more forgiving to aero changes than Hypercar. Coordinate wing with ride-height rake rather than tuning it in isolation. [single-source]
levers.Toe: More front toe-in -> better high-speed stability but more tire scrub/heat; toe-out -> sharper turn-in, less stable. Less rear toe-in -> better entry rotation but more rear instability; more rear toe-in -> a more stable rear on entry. [single-source, mostly LMP3]
levers.Brake bias: Bias too far forward -> entry understeer; too far rearward -> rear lockups, worse late-stint as rears fade. Target the most rearward bias the driver can control. [LMU] the default tends to run too far forward; moving rearward engages all four tires. Trim forward when tires are cold, rearward once warm. [broadly-agreed]
levers.Brake migration (Hypercar): [LMU] A separate system from static bias: as pedal pressure rises, bias shifts forward for braking-phase stability, then returns to the rearward static bias off the pedal. Running migration high (up to its 2.5% max) lets a driver keep a more-rearward static bias (more rotation) while still getting front stability under heavy braking. Risk: at max migration there's no front-shift headroom left if the rears start locking mid-race. [single-source]
levers.Traction control (TC): [LMU] Three axes: TC (overall level), TC slip (how much wheel slip is allowed before it intervenes — a little allowed slip is a real rotation tool), and TC cut (how hard power is cut once it activates). Higher TC -> safer but slower. TC cut mainly earns its keep in the wet (high cut lets you get back on throttle earlier); in the dry it's a stability margin costing some acceleration. Fixed setups run TC (esp. slip) higher than an open, well-tuned setup needs. [single-source]
levers.ABS (LMGT3 only): [LMU] LMGT3 is the only class with native ABS. It's a single 0-9 dial mixing activation timing AND front/rear bias-like behavior, not a simple more-is-safer scale: 1-3 tolerates more rear slip ('oversteer'), 4-6 balanced, 7-9 tolerates more front slip ('understeer'); the sub-value sets how early it activates. Pairing a rearward brake bias with a low ABS (1-3) makes the car easy to spin under braking; higher ABS can stabilize a lockup-prone car. [single-source, community]
